description_full: ZTO Express (Cayman) Inc. provides express delivery and other value-added logistics services in the People's Republic of China. It also offers less-than-truckload (LTL) logistics services; integrated logistics solutions for warehousing, distribution, and transportation; and freight forwarding services. The company was founded in 2002 and is headquartered in Shanghai, the People's Republic of China.
ceo_bio: Mr. Meisong  Lai | Founder, Chairman & CEO | Age 54 | Compensation: $249,768 (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 23K people. Revenue per employee of $309K ranks in the below the sector median among Industrials peers, with revenue growing 19%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $42K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $1K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: ZTO Express (Cayman) Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $15.2B market cap on $7.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 8% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 30%.

The business throws off $1.0B in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 42× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 5.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.0% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 21% operating margin runs 12pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.92x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.4% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 12% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.67, it is more defensive than the market.
About $40.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 26% in the 2020 crash and 46% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 59% below its DCF fair value of $49.14, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 35%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $38.66 to $63.68 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 11.1 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 0.4 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 15.0 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 45% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 25.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $27.50 on average, 35% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 8.1% by 14pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.26).
It runs a 30% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.32x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $539.3M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.3, in the safe zone).
It runs on negative working capital (-15 days), so customers and suppliers effectively fund its operations.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.1% over 3 years and 13.3% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 21.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 1.5x depreciation (10.6% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 27, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 8.6% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.0%, and institutions hold 13%.
It returns 5.0% a year to shareholders (1.2% in buybacks and 3.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 23,888 employees, each generates about $309K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 18.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $42K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $250K (1x revenue per employee).
